practical.title: Module 3.1 — Analyze and Implement Linear Search for Strings
practical.sourceActivity: Analyze and Implement Linear Search for Strings

coachingPrompts: What do you predict will happen before you run it?
What evidence shows that your change worked?
Can you explain the result in your own words?

teachingPlaylist.title: Run and Observe the Starter Program
teachingPlaylist.description: Execute the given main.c and note the printed output. Identify whether output matches intended semantics.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Become comfortable reading a small C program, running it, and mapping printed output back to code lines.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: We'll run the supplied main dot c. I will point out the includes, the linear search function that uses strcmp, and main's targets. Watch the two printed lines — do they match your expectation? If not, note the mismatch and where it comes from.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Compile and run: gcc -o main main.c && ./main. Expected output (starter): Target "Charlie" found at index 2. Target "Frank" found at index -1. The second line is wrong: it asserts found at index -1.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You receive a small C program from a teammate and must quickly verify it works for two test cases.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Run the program and write one sentence explaining why the second printed line is incorrect.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Assuming the compiler or strcmp is wrong — it's a logic/print swap in main, not a library bug.
teachingPlaylist.recap: We saw that the program compiled and ran but contained a message mismatch. Identifying where output maps to code is a key debugging skill.
codeSteps: Open main.c and locate the includes and the linear_search_strings function.
Run ./main and read the two output lines.
Find the if/else handling result2 and observe the printed messages.

teachingPlaylist.title: Make a Minimal Fix
teachingPlaylist.description: Swap the two printf lines for result2 so the printed messages match the condition.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Practice making minimal, precise edits and re-running to verify immediate effect.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Make a one-change fix: when result2 is not negative one we should print 'found' including the index; otherwise print 'not found'. Save, recompile, and run to see the corrected output.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Edit the two printf lines so the 'found' line is inside the result2 != -1 branch. Recompile and run; the second line should read 'Target "Frank" not found.'
teachingPlaylist.scenario: A test shows incorrect user-facing messages; you must change only the message placement without altering search logic.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Edit main.c, swap the two printfs in the result2 block, then run gcc -o main main.c && ./main and record the new output.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Replacing or rewriting the search function instead of fixing the print statements; keep changes minimal.
teachingPlaylist.recap: Small edits can resolve incorrect behavior quickly and safely when you understand which lines produce which outputs.
codeSteps: Open main.c to the second if-else block that handles result2.
Swap the two printf calls so the 'found' message prints when result2 != -1.
Save, compile and run to verify change.

teachingPlaylist.title: Add Case-Insensitive Search
teachingPlaylist.description: Implement linear_search_strings_case_insensitive and call it from main to find 'alice' when only 'Alice' exists.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Learn to extend existing code with a new function and integrate it into main for a real-world requirement (case-insensitive match).
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: We'll add a new function that mirrors the linear scan but uses strcasecmp to ignore case differences. This shows reuse of the same loop pattern with a different comparison operation.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Add int linear_search_strings_case_insensitive(...) using strcasecmp, then call it from main with target3 = "alice". Expected: Case-insensitive: Target "alice" found at index 0.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: Users type names in inconsistent case; your program should still find the correct name.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Add the new function and its call, then compile and run to confirm 'alice' maps to index 0.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Assuming strcmp can ignore case; you must use strcasecmp or normalize strings before comparing.
teachingPlaylist.recap: Extending by adding a small helper function keeps code organized and addresses a real user need.
codeSteps: Implement linear_search_strings_case_insensitive copying the loop pattern and using strcasecmp.
Call the new function from main with a lowercased target and print the result.

teachingPlaylist.title: Edge Cases and Big O Analysis
teachingPlaylist.description: Add tests for empty strings, duplicates, and very long strings. Then analyze best, worst, and average runtime taking string lengths into account.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Verify correctness under edge cases and practice precise Big O analysis that includes per-comparison cost.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Edge cases often break naive code. We'll add a few small experiments: searching for an empty string, finding the first occurrence among duplicates, and reasoning about a long string. Then explicitly state the answers for best, worst, and average complexity factoring in string length m.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: After adding tests, you'll see 'Searching empty string: result -1' and 'Duplicate test: first "Anna" at index 0'. Complexity answers: Best O(1), Worst O(n * m), Average O(n * m).
teachingPlaylist.scenario: A QA engineer asks you to reason about how the function scales when names get longer and the list grows.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Add the edge-case blocks, run the program, and write your answers for the three complexity questions before checking the solution.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Writing O(n) too quickly without accounting for the per-comparison cost of strcmp, which can be O(m).
teachingPlaylist.recap: Linear scan over n items with string comparisons of length m leads to O(n * m) worst-case. Good engineers always include per-comparison costs in their runtime reasoning.
codeSteps: Append tests in main for empty string and duplicates, and a small long-string experiment.
Compile and run, observe outputs for each case.
Answer: Best O(1), Worst O(n * m), Average O(n * m).

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.narratorGuide: Connect: An algorithm is a step-by-step recipe. Here the recipe searches a list of names for a given target. Observe: compile and run the supplied main dot c file using the exact commands below. When it runs, look closely at what the program prints for the second target — is that what you expected? Change: no code edits yet — only read output and predict why it's printed that way. Test: run the program and note the two lines printed. Explain: in your own words, point out which lines in main control each printed sentence. Pause and take a note before moving on.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.narratorGuide: Connect: Small, correct changes reduce bugs. Observe: you ran the program and saw a swapped message. Change: edit the second if-else block — when result2 is not -1, print the found message with index; otherwise print not found. Test: run gcc dash o main main dot c and then run dot slash main. Explain: check that the second line now reads 'Target "Frank" not found.' (because Frank is absent). Pause and write down the exact changed lines before continuing.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.narratorGuide: Connect: Real users type names in mixed case. Observe: the original search is case-sensitive and would not find "alice" if only "Alice" exists. Change: implement a case-insensitive search using strcasecmp or a manual lowercase comparison. Test: call this new function with target "alice" and print the index. Explain: compare outputs of case-sensitive and case-insensitive searches. Pause to predict the index before running.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.narratorGuide: Connect: Edge cases often reveal hidden assumptions. Observe: add tests — searching for an empty string, searching in a list with duplicates, and searching for a very long string. Change: run each case and watch the comparisons. Test: record outputs. Explain complexity: the linear scan does up to n comparisons, and each comparison (strcmp) can take up to m character comparisons, where m is the length of the strings compared. So worst-case time is O(n * m). Pause: write the best, worst, and average answers below before checking the provided solution.
